PRODUCT DIRECTION · OCTOBER 2026

Build a place.
Understand its life.

The interface should follow the player’s attention: a place first, an action second, details when they are useful. These four stages extend the interface concept into a coherent game without pretending the later systems already exist.

The first release

Board3 brings the production 3D composition engine into the approved world-first layout. It retains the shared browser Board library, card revisions, scene seeds, terrain-aware placement and undo. The scene tray is the explicit exception to the usual right-drawer rule. Detailed controls stay on the right; navigation stays on the left.

It shares the current saved Board with Sandbox2. Saving from either surface changes that same world in this browser. There is no automatic replacement of an existing world, no migration to a new save format, and no cloud-save promise.

1
THIS RELEASE · COMPOSITION FOUNDATION

Compose a place

Start on the landscape. Choose a remembered scene from a compact illustrated tray and place it directly. Select a placed scene to inspect or revise it; enter close-up only by choice. The world remains the context for every decision.

  • Real scene geometry and recipes, shared saved cards, rotation, movement, removal, undo and redo.
  • Keep each family’s loaded seed, preset and dressing while switching between scenes.
  • Show invalid placement and save failure honestly. Preserve the last committed world when generation or placement fails.
  • Frame the settlement separately from the whole region. Keep touch targets usable and the canvas visible beside drawers.

Exit test: on a phone, choose, place, inspect, move, undo, save and reload a scene without needing a close-up first. MCP must observe the same world and use the same mutation functions.

2
NEXT · EXISTING PARTS, INCOMPLETE INTEGRATION

Make life understandable

Turn visible activity into understandable cause and effect. Select a worker, building or route to see what it is doing, what it needs and where a delivery is going. Put the answer beside its subject; reserve totals and long explanations for the inspector.

  • Reconcile the current spatial visits, town routines and Board economy into one inspectable model.
  • Keep the default world self-managing: care, food and replenishment should recover without survival micromanagement. Account for outside support explicitly.
  • Offer temporary access, delivery and work overlays with clear sources and timestamps. A drawn road alone must not imply verified travel.
  • Use quiet, contextual notices for interruptions. Pause, step and speed controls must share typed MCP actions.

Exit test: a player can follow one complete job and identify why it paused. Long runs remain balanced and recover from interruption; observation never invents production. The current path activity and layout connection counts are only a starting point.

3
PLANNED · AUTHORED PLAY

Let the world teach the game

Build the first watchable farm → harvest → market reveal → sale → neighboring farm loop. New possibilities appear in the world at the moment they become useful. The interface explains the next decision through visible consequences.

  • Introduce each action through the place it affects, with recoverable mistakes and explicit rewards.
  • Keep sandbox autonomy distinct from scenario rules. Scarcity is an intentional scenario setting, never a punishment for looking away.
  • Preserve mage tower, overwatch and fairy castle in the direction. Their eventual world effects need explicit rules and balancing; no effect values are assumed here.
  • Make progression, unlocks and resource changes inspectable through the same state and action contracts.

Exit test: a new player completes the narrow farm-to-market loop without a separate tutorial manual, can explain the outcome, and can resume a saved game without duplicate rewards.

4
EXPLORATION · GENERATIVE CREATION

Create worlds worth keeping

Let players request characters, assets and spontaneous new biomes, then make those creations coherent members of their world. Voice becomes another way to issue the same understandable actions.

  • Review generated assets through the existing asset pipeline: scale, origin, bounds, entrances, placement clearance and supported uses.
  • Separate appearance from capability. Generated geometry does not automatically gain production, jobs or ecological behavior.
  • Preview biome transitions and consequences before adoption. Preserve seeds, versions and provenance so worlds remain reproducible.
  • Map voice requests to discoverable typed actions with target, revision, undo and clear confirmation for consequential changes.

Exit test: create one reviewed asset or biome, place it, save it and reproduce it. Providers, costs, ecological rules, wider gameplay and persistence policy remain design decisions.

How we judge the interface

QuestionEvidence to collect
Is the world still the main subject?Desktop and phone screenshots during selection, placement, inspection and error recovery.
Can people discover the action?First-use task completion, wrong turns, assistance needed and time spent searching controls.
Do people understand the consequence?Ask them to predict placement, production and undo outcomes before acting.
Can the system be trusted?Save/reload round trips, failure rollback, stale-command rejection and receipts linked to fresh MCP captures.

These are proposed evaluation criteria, not completed user-study results. Learn from Anno’s task-oriented information hierarchy and Civilization’s decision overlays; use in-world presentation where it improves comprehension, not as a rule that forbids all menus.

Open Board3 · Open Sandbox2

Delivered capabilities and future design remain separate. This page is the Board3 roadmap; the shared drawing principles and semantic world contracts remain authoritative for implementation.
